Due to the nature of this provision, which sets out the subject matter of the Directive in general terms, implementation was not considered necessary.

As a general preliminary remark, please note that the Directive has been implemented into Dutch law through the Act of 15 May 2019, Staatsblad 2019, 180 (entry into force 1 June 2019, Staatsblad 2019, 181). The full title in Dutch of this implementing Act is Wet van 15 mei 2019 tot wijziging van het Wetboek van Strafvordering en de Overleveringswet ter implementatie van richtlijn nr. 2016/800/EU van het Europees Parlement en de Raad van 11 mei 2016 betreffende procedurele waarborgen voor kinderen die verdachte of beklaagde zijn in een strafprocedure (PbEU L 132). The underlying parliamentary dossier is numbered 35116 and publicly available on zoek.officielebekendmakingen.nl.

In this Transposition Table references will be made only to the consolidated versions of applicable laws.


As a second preliminary remark, note that the term 'suspect' in this table may refer to the suspect or the accused, or both, depending on the context. This corresponds to the Dutch legal terminology, in which persons suspected of a crime are called 'suspects', both before and after indictment.

items.text: 1. This Directive applies to children who are suspects or accused persons in criminal proceedings. It applies until the final determination of the question whether the suspect or accused person has committed a criminal offence, including, where applicable, sentencing and the resolution of any appeal.

provisions.comment: Translation borrowed from: http://www.ejtn.eu/PageFiles/6533/2014%20seminars/Omsenie/WetboekvanStrafvordering_ENG_PV.pdf. Unofficial translation; official translation not available.
provisions.textEn: The provisions of this Chapter shall apply to persons who, at the time of the commission of the offence, had not yet reached the age of eighteen years, insofar as the provisions of this Chapter do not derogate therefrom.

items.comment: Book 4 of the Dutch Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP) envisages in Title II a number of provisions that specifically apply to criminal proceedings against minor suspects. The Title starts with Article 488 CCP, stipulating, first, in paragraph 1 that the provisions of the CCP shall apply insofar as no explicit derogation have been provided for, and, secondly in paragraph 2 that the provisions in this title apply to suspects below the age of 18 years old at the time of the commission of the offence. As will follow from this transposition table, explicit implementing provisions have been added to this title. As such, Article 488 CCP concerns an indirect implementation of Article 2(1) of the Directive.

items.text: 2. This Directive applies to children who are requested persons from the time of their arrest in the executing Member State, in accordance with Article 17.
items.comment: See the information below on the transposition of Article 17 of the Directive; the requirement envisaged in this provision follows from the provision implementing Article 17.

items.text: 3. With the exception of Article 5, point (b) of Article 8(3), and Article 15, insofar as those provisions refer to a holder of parental responsibility, this Directive, or certain provisions thereof, applies to persons as referred to in paragraphs 1 and 2 of this Article, where such persons were children when they became subject to the proceedings but have subsequently reached the age of 18, and the application of this Directive, or certain provisions thereof, is appropriate in the light of all the circumstances of the case, including the maturity and vulnerability of the person concerned. Member States may decide not to apply this Directive when the person concerned has reached the age of 21.

transp.label: No national implementation (either officially nor de facto/indirect)

items.comment: It was decided not to make use of the exception this provisions allows of. Such would have been contrary to Article 488 of the Dutch Code of Criminal Procedure, a provision that falls under the code's chapter that envisages rules regarding criminal proceedings against suspects below the age of 18 years old. Article 488 currently does not envisage such a limitation as allowed for under the Directive (Article 488(2) reads as follows: The provisions of this Chapter shall apply to persons who, at the time of the commission of the offence, had not yet reached the age of eighteen years, insofar as the provisions of this Chapter do not derogate therefrom). To nevertheless apply such a limitation, by means of adjusting Article 488 would have resulted in a lower level of protection of rights for children which was considered undesirable by the Dutch legislator.

items.heading: Article 4

provisions.comment:

In addition to the rights provided for under Article 4 of the Directive, the Dutch implementing provision further envisages a right for children to be informed about the possibility to make audiovisual recordings of hearings (Article 488(1)(c). The reference to Article 488ac clarifies that in deciding on whether such recordings will indeed be made, the seriousness of the offence and the personality of the suspect play a role - that is to say that the seriousness of the offence or the personality of the suspect may give rise to the decision to actually make such recordings.
provisions.textEn:
1. Without prejudice to the provisions of Articles 27c and 27ca, the suspect shall immediately upon arrest be informed: a) that his parents or guardian will be notified of his deprivation of liberty, if ordered; b) of his right to be accompanied by his parents or guardian, or by a confidant, during stages of the proceedings other than court hearings, pursuant to Article 488ab; c) of the possibility to make audiovisual recordings of hearings, pursuant to Article 488ac; d) of the right to a medical examination, pursuant to Article 489a; e) of the right to an advice on his personality and living conditions, pursuant to Article 494a.
  2. Upon being summoned for questioning, pursuant to Article 491a, the suspect shall be informed of his right to be accompanied by his parents or guardian, or by a confidant.
  3. Upon being summoned for questioning, pursuant to Article 493(4), the suspect shall be informed of: a) the right to have the duration of pre-trial detention determined at a length as short as appropriately possible and the possibility of a stay of execution of the pre-trial detention order, pursuant to Article 493(1); b) the right to be accompanied by the parents or guardian, or by a confidant; c) the right to periodical assessments of pre-trial detention; d) the right to be held separately from adults while kept in pre-trial detention.
  4. Upon the indictment being served, the suspect shall be informed of: a) the obligation to appear in person at trial, pursuant to Article 495a; b) the right to have his case dealt with behind closed doors, pursuant to Article 495b; c) the right to be accompanied during court hearings by his parents or guardian, or by a confidant, pursuant to Article 496.
  5. The notification of rights shall be given in simple and accessible language. If the suspect does not, or not sufficiently, speak or understand Dutch, the information shall be given in a language he understands.

items.comment:
The following explanations apply to Article 4(1) of the Directive in its entirety. This provision distinguishes between the moment that children have been made aware that they are suspects or accused persons (letter a) and the earliest appropriate stage in the proceedings (letter b). Moreover, upon deprivation of liberty, children must be informed about a number of additional rights, i.e. those provided for under Article 12 of the Directive (letter c). The official position of the Ministry of Justice and Security is that the implementation in Article 488aa(1)-(4) amounts to the same. This provision distinguishes between the moment of arrest (par. 1), the moment that the child has been summoned to be questioned with a view to the intention of the public prosecutor to impose a penalty order (par. 2), the moment that the child has been summoned to be questioned with a view to decisions regarding pre-trial detention (par. 3), and, finally the moment of being summoned to trial proceedings (par. 4).

Regarding the first moment, i.e. the moment of arrest, Article 488aa(1) explicitly refers to Articles 27c and 27ca of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Consequently, the provisions implementing the relevant provisions of Directive 2012/13/EU on the right to information and Directive 2013/48/EU on the right of access to a lawyer apply in this stage too.

Although structured and worded differently from the Directive, we have found no significant gaps between Article 4(1) of the Directive and Article 488aa of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Where potential questions of deviation arise, this will be mentioned in a comment on the applicable paragraph of letter of Article 4(1) of the Directive.

items.subHeading: Right of the child to have the holder of parental responsibility informed

In order to meet the requirements of Article 5 of the Directive, the original text of Article 488b has been amended.
provisions.textEn:
1. In derogation of Article 27e(1), the assistant public prosecutor to have ordered the suspect's detention for investigation at the arraignment shall notify the parents or guardian of the deprivation of liberty and the reasons for it as soon as possible. The parents or guardian shall furthermore receive a notification of the rights provided for in Article 488aa.
  2. The notification of rights provided for in the first paragraph, shall not take place when: (a) this would contrary to the interests of the suspect; (b) the notification is not possible because despite reasonable efforts the parents or guardian cannot be reached or identified.
  3. In the case referred to in paragraph 2, the information shall be provided to a confidant. If no confidant has been nominated, the information shall be provided to the Child Care and Protection Board.
  4. Where the circumstances, referred to in paragraph 2, cease to exist, the information shall be provided to the parents or guardian.

provisions.comment: Own translation; no official translation available.
provisions.textEn: The assistant public prosecutor may postpone the notification as per the first and second paragraphs insofar and for as long as justified by an urgent need to: (a) avert serious adverse consequences for the life, liberty or physical integrity of a person or (b) prevent substantial damage to the investigation.

In other words, there is no single, specific implementing provision in this regard. Specifically, Article 6(3) of the Directive finds implementation in Articles 28, 28b, 28c and 489 of the CCP (the first three provisions already being in place to implement Directive 2013/48/EU). Nor does the Dutch legislator distinguish between the various subparagraphs of Article 6(3) - a, b, c and d - regarding the provision's implementation.


Article 28 CCP provides for a general right of access to a lawyer in criminal proceedings, 'in the manner stipulated in the CCP'; Article 28b provides for the right of access to a lawyer without undue delay after deprivation of liberty, i.e. arrest (as follows from the transposition table with respect to Article 2(1) of Directive 2013/48/EU, the CCP does not expressly provide for the right of the suspect or accused not to have deprived of their liberty of access to a lawyer prior to questioning; see in this regard also the comments made with respect to Article 3(4) of Directive 2013/48/EU); and Article 28c provides for the right of the suspect of accused to have been deprived of their liberty (arrested) of access to a lawyer prior to police questioning (and which should be read in conjunction with Article 28b; see the comments made with respect to Article 3(2)(a) of Directive 2013/48/EU). According to the Dutch legislator when implementing Article 3 of Directive 2013/48/EU, of all of the 'points in time' provided for in Article 3(2) of the Directive, in the Netherlands, arrest is the earliest. In the Netherlands, therefore, the earliest point in time at which the authorities are required to take active steps to ensure that the suspect or accused may exercise their right of access to a lawyer is immediately after arrest. To this end, Article 28b was newly introduced into the Dutch Code of Criminal Procedure when Directive 2013/48/EU was implemented. Article 489 of the Code of Criminal Procedure has been added in order to meet the implementing requirements of the Directive at hand, i.e. Directive 2016/800.

items.comment:
For the suspect or accused to have been deprived of their liberty (arrested), the right has been expressly implemented with respect to questioning by the police (in Article 28c of the Dutch Code of Criminal Procedure (hereafter: CCP), in conjunction with Article 28b thereof); for the suspect of accused not to have been deprived of their liberty, the right is considered to be implicit in the CCP, and was therefore not expressly transposed. See in this regard the comments made above with respect to Articles 2(1) and 3(2) of Directive 2013/48/EU on the right of access to a lawyer.


Article 28c CCP provides for a right of access to a lawyer prior to police questioning in respect of suspects or accused persons who have been arrested and for whom, pursuant to Article 28b CCP, a lawyer is available. The maximum duration of such access is thirty minutes.


As apparent from Article 28b CCP, in the Netherlands, what is required on the part of the authorities by way of 'active steps' to ensure that the right of the suspect or accused of access to a lawyer prior to questioning may be exercised (see in this regard the comments made in the transposition tabble on Directive 2013/48/EU, with respect to Article 2(1) of that Directive), is dependent on the seriousness of the crime of which the person concerned is suspected as well as the vulnerability of the person concerned (the more serious the crime and the more vulnerable the person concerned, the more is required by way of active steps on the part of the authorities). Pursuant to Article 28b(1) CCP, in respect of vulnerable suspects or accused persons or persons suspected or accused of crimes punishable by twelve years' imprisonment or more, who have been arrested and in respect of whom 'detention for investigation' (ophouden voor onderzoek; a coercive measure principally aimed at, but not limited to, questioning; see Article 56a CCP) has been ordered, the assistant public prosecutor (to have made the order) is required to inform the Legal Aid Board (raad voor rechtsbijstand) of the arrest immediately (regardless of whether the person concerned has requested legal assistance), so that the Board can assign the suspect or accused a lawyer. Pursuant to Article 28b(2) CCP, in respect of persons suspected or accused of crimes for which pre-trial detention is permitted (typically in respect of persons suspected or accused of crimes punishable by four years' imprisonment or more), who have been arrested and in respect of whom 'detention for investigation' has been ordered, upon such a person's request (in reply to a question put to them), the assistant public prosecutor is required to inform the Legal Aid Board (raad voor rechtsbijstand) of the arrest immediately (regardless of whether the person concerned has requested legal assistance), so that the Board can assign the suspect or accused a lawyer. Neither provision obliges the suspect or accused person to make use of a legal aid lawyer, however; if they wish to make use of their own lawyer, they may do so, on the understanding that they finance such assistance themselves and provided that lawyer is available promptly. Pursuant to Article 28b(3) CCP, in respect of arrested persons suspected or accused of crimes for which pre-trial detention is not permitted, the authorities are required to give them the opportunity to contact a lawyer themselves (i.e. not through the Legal Aid Board), but only if, in reply to a question put to them, they have requested legal assistance.


While the Dutch legislator's position - in implementing Directive 2013/48/EU - was that this 'set up' is in compliance with the Directive, the Dutch Bar Association in particular was critical in this regard during the legislative process. In particular, it was critical of the half hour maximum. In response to this criticism, the legislator observed that, thus far, this had not been especially problematic in practice, and that the Directive did not preclude Member States from setting a time frame in this regard. It may be assumed that the same position was taken with regard to the Directive at hand on the rights of children in criminal proceedings.

provisions.textEn:
1. Save for the restrictions to be established under paragraphs 2, 3 and 4, the juvenile shall have a right to send and receive letters and items by post. The costs involved shall be for the juvenile's account unless the governor determines otherwise.

2. The governor shall have the authority to examine envelopes or other postal items sent by or intended for juveniles for the presence of enclosed objects and to open them for that purpose. If the envelopes or other postal items are sent by or are intended for the persons or bodies referred to in Article 42, paragraph 1 or 2, this examination shall be carried out in the presence of the juvenile involved.

3. The governor shall have the authority to exercise supervision over the letters and postal items sent by or intended for juveniles with a view to the interests set out in the fourth paragraph. This supervision may comprise the copying of letters or other postal items. The juveniles shall be notified beforehand of the way in which supervision will be exercised.

4. The governor may refuse to distribute certain letters or other postal items as well as enclosed objects if this is necessary with a view to the following interests:

a. the maintenance of order or safety in the institution;

b. the protection of public order or national security;

c. the prevention or investigation of criminal offences;

d. the protection of victims of, or those involved otherwise in criminal offences;

e. the execution of the perspective plan.

5. The governor shall ensure that the letters or other postal items or enclosed objects that are not distributed are either returned to the juvenile or sent at his expense to the sender or to an address given by the juvenile, or placed in safekeeping for the juvenile with issue of a receipt, or destroyed with the juvenile's consent, or handed to a law enforcement officer with a view to the prevention or investigation of criminal offences.

1. Article 41, paragraphs 3 and 4, shall not apply to letters addressed by the juvenile to, or sent by:

a. members of the Royal Family;

c. Our Minister;

d. judicial authorities;

e. the National Ombudsman;

f. public health inspectors;

g. the Central Council for the Execution of Criminal Law, or members thereof;

h. the Supervisory Committee or a Complaints Committee, or members thereof;

i. his legal aid provider;

j. his probation officer or officers of the certified institution;

k. his parents or guardian, step parents or foster parents, unless compelling interests of the juvenile dictate otherwise;

l. other persons or bodies designated by Our Minister or the governor.

2. For the purposes of paragraph 1(d), judicial authorities shall also mean organs that have the authority under the law or a treaty valid in the Netherlands to be notified of complaints or to review matters initiated by a complaint.

3. Our Minister may establish further rules concerning the sending of letters to or by the persons and bodies referred to in paragraph 1.

During this visit they can freely converse with the juvenile, except when the governor is of the opinion, following consultation with the visitor in question, that the juvenile poses a serious risk to the visitor's safety. In that case, the governor shall disclose before the visit which supervisory measures will be taken, so that the conversation can take place as undisturbed as possible. items.comment:
For the implementation of this provision, the Dutch legislator relied on the implementing provisions of Article 3(3) of Directive 2013/48/EU. In that respect, regarding the right to have a lawyer present and participate during questioning by the judicial authorities, according to the Dutch legislator, this right was already provided for in the Dutch Code of Criminal Procedure (hereafter: CCP), albeit impliedly, at the time of implementation, and no amendments or supplements were necessary in this regard in light of the Directive. In making this finding, the legislator referred to the ability of the examining magistrate/investigating judge to put questions to the suspect or accused in the context of police custody (inverzekeringstelling), pre-trial detention (voorlopige hechtenis) and the investigating judge's own investigations, and of the trial judge in the course of the trial proceedings. According to the legislator, the relevant provisions in the CCP (Articles 28, 57(2), 59a(2), 63(4), 65(1) in conjunction with 23(3), 86(2), 186a and 331(1)) imply the presence and participation of the suspect or accused's lawyer. Pursuant to Article 488 CCP, these provisions equally apply in criminal proceedings where the suspect is a child.


Regarding the right to have a lawyer present and participate during questioning by the law enforcement authorities - the police - explicit transposition was required in this regard. Article 28d(1) of the CCP, which was newly introduced into the CCP for the purpose of implementing the Directive, provides for a general right of the suspect or accused to have a lawyer present and participate during police questioning, regardless of whether they have been deprived of their liberty. Regardless of whether the suspect or accused person has been deprived of their liberty, the authorities are required to take active steps to make exercise of the right to have a lawyer present and participate during questioning possible. According to the Dutch legislator, this is different for the right of access to a lawyer prior to police questioning.


Pursuant to Article 28d(1) CCP, the authorities - the interrogating officer - are only required to allow a lawyer to be present and participate during questioning when the suspect or accused person has requested them do so. The interrogating officer may refuse a request on the part of the suspect or accused to consult with their lawyer during questioning, if granting repeated requests in this regard would be result in disruption.


Pursuant to Article 28d(4) CCP, which provides for the adoption of delegated legislation in the form of a Legislative Decree concerning the format of, and the preservation of order during, questioning, the Decree on Format of and Order During Police Questioning (Besluit inrichting en orde politieverhoor) was adopted. According to the Dutch legislator, regulation of the participation of a lawyer during police questioning was necessary, given that in the Netherlands, such participation is a relatively new phenomenon. For this position, the Dutch legislator - at the time of implementing Directive 2013/48/EU - relied on Recital 25 of Directive 2013/48/EU, pursuant to which Member States are permitted to regulate the participation of a lawyer during police questioning, provided that such procedures do not prejudice the effective exercise and essence of the right concerned. While there was broad consensus during the legislative process that the participation of a lawyer during police questioning should be regulated, the manner of participation was (and continues to be) the subject of (sometimes heated) debate in the Netherlands. While the Police envisaged a more passive role for the lawyer, the Dutch Bar Association envisaged a more active role in this regard. The Decree aims to strike a balance between the two positions. The relevant provisions are translated below; because there continues to be (legitimate) discussion as to the compatibility of the Decree with the Directive and the case law of the ECtHR in this regard, we have marked Article 28d CCP and the provisions of the Decree that in our view are the most problematic from the perspective that the right should be effective as 'partially implemented'. At the same time, it should be noted here that the picture to emerge from practice is that of a working method that is more accommodating (and less skeptical) of the role of defence counsel during questioning than the Decree itself would imply.

This investigative act is not expressly provided for in the Dutch Code of Criminal Procedure (hereafter: CCP). It may, however, be applied in the context of other investigative acts which are expressly provided for therein, for example, the schouw, i.e. the 'site inspection', as provided for in Articles 151, 192, 193 and 318 CCP, the first three provisions providing for the schouw in the investigative phase, the latter providing for the schouw in the trial phase), in which context the suspect or accused was already entitled to legal assistance (the relevant provisions are Articles 151(2) and (3), 193 and 318; the latter provision does not provide for the right of legal assistance, but for the 'temporary relocation' of the trial to another site than the court building, during which time the accused present is entitled to the same legal assistance/representation as they are in the court building). According to the Dutch legislator with respect to this provision's equivalent in Directive 2013/48/EU, no amendments or supplementing was required in this regard. The position of the Dutch legislator with respect to Article 6(4)(c) of the Directive at hand (2016/800/EU) was unchanged.


In the course of implementing Article 3(3)(c) of Directive 2013/4/8EU, regarding the power of the authorities to deny the suspect or accused and their lawyer access to the schouw, the Dutch legislator has pointed to Recital 26 of Directive 2013/48/EU, pursuant to which '[s]uspects or accused persons have the right for their lawyer to attend investigative or evidence-gathering acts … in so far as the suspects or accused persons are required or permitted to attend'. 


Another context in which the 'confrontation' envisgaed here may be applied is the questioning of a witness at trial, at which the accused will normally be present. Insofar as this qualifies as a confrontation in the aforementioned sense, the right of the accused to have their lawyer attend the confrontation flows from Article 28(1) CCP, which provides for the right of the suspect or accused of legal representation at all stages of criminal proceedings, including the trial stage. According to the Dutch legislator in the implementation process of Directive 23013/48/EU, the 'single confrontation' (enkelvoudige confrontatie, not be confused with the meervoudige confrontatie, i.e. the identity parade, addressed above), an investigative act entailing the observation by a witness of the suspect's appearance in order to ascertain whether that person was involved in the crime also falls under the definition of confrontation in Directive 2013/48/EU, and hence also in Directive 2016/800/EU, for which purpose it was necessary to amend the Decree on the Application of Measures in the Interests of the Investigation (Besluit toepassing maatregelen in het belang van het onderzoek) to allow for counsel to be able to 'follow', i.e. monitor, the single confrontation.

1. Letters or other documents which are subject to the duty of secrecy of persons who have the right to assert privilege, as referred to in Articles 218 and 218a, shall not be seized from them, unless with their consent. The investigating judge is authorized to make this determination.
  2. If a person who has the right to assert privilege objects to the seizure of letters or other documents because they are subject to the duty of secrecy, they shall not be examined until the investigating judge has issued a decision on the objection.
  3.   5. Unless such persons have consented to a search, a search shall only be conducted at their premises insofar as this search can be conducted without violating clerical secrecy, professional privilege or official secrecy and it shall not include letters or documents other than those which are the subject of the criminal offence or have been used in its commission.

To our assessment, this provision has only been transposed implicitly, meaning that the essence of it is implied by a number of both implementing provisions and provisions that were already in force. First of all, the wording of (the newly adopted) Article 494b of the Dutch Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP) implies that the advice (given pursuant to Article 494 CCP) must serve the authorities in taking a decision on sentencing; after all, Article 494b CCP stipulates that both in punishment orders and judgments it must mentioned how the advice (given pursuant to Article 494 CCP) was taken into account when deciding on the sanction or measure imposed on the child. Secondly, the wordings of Articles 77s(2) and 77w(2) of the Dutch Criminal Code (CC) clearly express that the required advice must serve the imposition of sanctions. As to other sanctions, such as conditional imprisonment, it is standing practice (without codification, however) that judges are given the required advice, precisely to be of use in determining on the specific conditions to impose. Outside sentencing, it must be underlined that this also applies with regard to decisions suspending pre-trial detention and the conditions that are usually imposed in that respect. On the latter, see comments below with respect to paragraph 7.


In practice, the various occurrences of individual assessment (whether codified or not) are being executed by using the services of the 'National Set of Instruments Juvenile Justice System' (Landelijk Instrumentarium Jeugd, hereinafter: LJI). The LJI comprises a set of tools designed for children aged 12-17 who allegedly committed a crime. The set of tools has been developed for use by various partners in the youth criminal justice chain and support the structred gathering and analysis of information regarding the child. On the basis of that information, the LIJ maps the probability of a repeat offense as well as the needs for care, in order to advice on an appropriate (care) intervention for the child involved. During the legislative procedure, the Council for the Judiciary (Raad voor de Rechtspraak) raised the question whether the so-called accelerated procedure would require to be changed becaue of the requirement of Article 7(5) of the Directive to carry out an individual assessment before indictment. The accelerated procedure (in Dutch known as the ZSM-werkwijze, in which ZSM stands for As Fast, Smart, Selective, Simple, Together and Societally Targeted as Possible) enables the public prosecutor and the national police, in collaboration with chain partners (such as the Probation Service and the Child Care and Protection Board), to decide very quickly on if and how to further handle a case, e,g, whether it should result in an out-of-court-settlement or be further investigated and, potentially, brought before the court. As pointed out by the Council for the Judiciary, it is common practice in such accelerated procedures that a potential individual assessment only follows after a decision has been taken on which route to follow, and, hence, potentially only after the precise intervention or settlement has already been decided on. This logically follows from the very aim of the accelerated procedure to act quickly. However, it was raised whether such common practice would be allowed for under Article 7(5) of the Directive. The question has not been answered explicitly by the Ministry of Justice and Security in its explanatory memorandum to the Implementing Act; it merely held that it considered Dutch law to sufficiently take into account the findings of individual assessments in the course of criminal proceedings against children.

provisions.textEn:
1. The assistant public prosecutor to have ordered the suspect’s detention for investigation may either ex officio, or upon request of the suspect, his lawyer, his parent or guardian, or his confidant, order a medical examination of the suspect, with a view to the determination of his capacity to be subjected to questioning or an investigative act. A medical examination assesses the overall mental and physical condition of the suspect. The examination shall be as non-invasive as possible.
  2. A medical examination shall be carried out by a physician or under the responsibility of a physician.
  3. Where the conclusion of a medical examination requires so, the questioning of the suspect or the subjecting of him to an investigative act for the purpose of evidence-gathering, may be postponed.

Where a medical examination has been carried out, the conclusion of that examination shall be recorded in writing.

items.text: 1. Member States shall ensure that children who are deprived of liberty have the right to a medical examination without undue delay with a view, in particular, to assessing their general mental and physical condition. The medical examination shall be as non-invasive as possible and shall be carried out by a physician or another qualified professional.

provisions.comment:
Own translation; no official translation available.


According to the Dutch legislator, the mentioning of the assistant public prosecutor's order to detain the suspect for investigation marks the fact that the right to a medical examination applies as of the moment of deprivation of liberty. The two other phrases in bold mark two other aspects that constitute (almost literal) transpositions of Article 8(1) of the Directive.
provisions.textEn: The assistant public prosecutor to have ordered the suspect’s detention for investigation may either ex officio, or upon request of the suspect, his lawyer, his parent or guardian, or his confidant, order a medical examination of the suspect, with a view to the determination of his capacity to be subjected to questioning or an investigative act. A medical examination assesses the overall mental and physical condition of the suspect. The examination shall be as non-invasive as possible.

provisions.comment:
Own translation; no official translation available.


This implementing provision ensures that medical examinations are carried out by qualified professionals. The phrase 'under the responsibility of a physician' refers to the possibility that examinations are carried out by an assistant physician, or by a nurse.
provisions.textEn: A medical examination shall be carried out by a physician or under the responsibility of a physician.

items.text: 2. The results of the medical examination shall be taken into account when determining the capacity of the child to be subject to questioning, other investigative or evidence-gathering acts, or any measures taken or envisaged against the child.

items.heading: Article 9
items.comment:
Prior to the adoption of the Directive, Dutch law on criminal procedure did not not provide yet for a codified right to audiovisual recording of questioning of children. However, under the Decree on auditory and audiovisual recording of questioning declarants, witnesses and suspects it was standing practice to safeguard the right to audiovisual recording of questioning children as provided for in the Directive. With the entry into force of the Implementing Act, this standing practice has now been codified under Article 488ac of the Dutch Code of Criminal Procedure.


For those who wish to consult the aforementioned Decree, the latest version has been published in the Official Gazette 2018, 60346, available online (In Dutch only) at: https://zoek.officielebekendmakingen.nl/stcrt-2018-60346.html. In order to meet the requirements of Directive 2012/29/EU on the rights of victims of crime, it has been amended in 2018. These amendments bear no relevance for the matter at hand.

items.text: 1. Member States shall ensure that questioning of children by police or other law enforcement authorities during the criminal proceedings is audio-visually recorded where this is proportionate in the circumstances of the case, taking into account, inter alia, whether a lawyer is present or not and whether the child is deprived of liberty or not, provided that the child's best interests are always a primary consideration.

provisions.comment:
Own translation; no official translation available.


The proportionality assessment allowed for in Article 9(1) of the Directive has also been envisaged in this implementing provision. This also corresponds with the aforementioned Decree on auditory and audiovisual recording of questioning declarants, witnesses and suspects (see introductory comments with respect to Article 9 of the Directive). However, in contrast to the Directive, audiovisual recording of the questioning has not been made dependent on whether a lawyer is present or not. According to the explanatory memorandum to the act implementing the Directive, it was argued that such an exception to the rule of adiovisual recording would have entailed a change of current practice and, furthermore, that the right to have a lawyer present constitutes a fundamental point of departure for children in criminal proceedings and should not provide a reason not to audio-visually record the questioning of a child.
provisions.textEn: The investigating officer shall audio-visually record the questioning if the seriousness of the crime or the personality of the suspect so requires.

items.text: 2. In the absence of audiovisual recording, questioning shall be recorded in another appropriate manner, such as by written minutes which are duly verified.
items.comment: The official position of the Ministry of Justice and Security, and as apparently supported by parliament, is that the requirement of Article 9(2) of the Directive follows from Article 29a(1) of the Dutch Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP) which was already in force prior to the adoption of the Directive. Article 29a(1) CCP stipulates that written notes are made up in a police record (proces-verbaal) of all questionings, and that such a record must also state whether audiovisual recordings have been made.

items.text: 3. This Article shall be without prejudice to the possibility to ask questions for the sole purpose of the identification of the child without audiovisual recording.

items.heading: Article 10
items.comment:
In fact, this provision has in part been transposed explicitly. For the remaining part, the official position of the Ministry of Justice and Security - a position that has apparently been supported by parliament - is that the existing provisions on pre-trial detention already meet the requirements of Article 10 of the Directive.


Below, the existing provisions will be set out first. It concerns Articles 58, 59a, 64, and 65 of the Dutch Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP). Note that these provisions have been made applicable on criminal proceedings against children too, i.e. under Article 488 CCP (see comments made with respect to Article 2(1) of the Directive). They concern various stages of pre-trial detention:

  1. Articles 58 and 59 CCP concern the first stage of police custody (inverzekeringstelling)
  2. Article 64 concerns the second stage of remand in custody (inbewaringstelling)
  3. Article 65 concern the stages of remand detention (gevangenhouding) or arrest (gevangenneming).

As will follow (see the parts in bold) prescribe maximum terms for detention, and accordingly terms for periodic review, and require court involvement. Prior to any decision taken, suspects must always be heard by the competent court. Such hearings provide the opportunity for the suspect or his lawyer to request for release.

and the changes made to Article 493 CCP.


In order to meet all requirements of the Directive, it was considered necessary to amend Article 493 CCP. This provision comprehends additional rules for criminal proceedings where the suspect is a child. The parts in bold (see below) clarify which parts of the provisions concern explicit transpositions of Article 10 of the Directive.

items.text: 1. Member States shall ensure that deprivation of liberty of a child at any stage of the proceedings is limited to the shortest appropriate period of time. Due account shall be taken of the age and individual situation of the child, and of the particular circumstances of the case.

Translation partly borrowed from: http://www.ejtn.eu/PageFiles/6533/2014%20seminars/Omsenie/WetboekvanStrafvordering_ENG_PV.pdf. Unofficial translation; official translation not available.


The part in bold explicitly transposed the first sentence of Article 10(1) of the Directive.
provisions.textEn: Pre-trial detention shall be determined at the shortest appropriate period of time. If the court orders the pre-trial detention of the suspect, it shall consider whether the enforcement of this order may be suspended, either immediately, or after a specific period of time. In doing so, the court may charge a foundation, as referred to in Article 1 of the Youth Care Act, or if the suspect has reached the age of sixteen years, a probation service, as referred to in Article 14d(2) of the Criminal Code, to carry out the supervision of conditions imposed on him, and, to that end, to provide support to the suspect

provisions.comment:
Own translation; no official translation available.


This paragraph explicitly transposes the second sentence of Article 10(1) of the Directive.
provisions.textEn: The judge shall take account of the age and the person of the offender, and of the circumstances under which the alleged offence has been committed.

items.comment: In fact, this first paragraph of Article 10 of the Directive has been transposed explicitly, i.e. through amendments made to Article 493 of the Dutch Code of Criminal Procedure.

items.text: 2. Member States shall ensure that deprivation of liberty, in particular detention, shall be imposed on children only as a measure of last resort. Member States shall ensure that any detention is based on a reasoned decision, subject to judicial review by a court. Such a decision shall also be subject to periodic review, at reasonable intervals of time, by a court, either ex officio or at the request of the child, of the child's lawyer, or of a judicial authority which is not a court. Without prejudice to judicial independence, Member States shall ensure that decisions to be taken pursuant to this paragraph are taken without undue delay.

This provision concerns the stage of police custody.
provisions.textEn:
1. The police custody order shall only be issued in the case of a criminal offence for which pre-trial detention is permitted.

2. The police custody order shall only be in effect for a maximum of three days. In the case of urgent necessity, the public prosecutor may extend it one time for a maximum of three days.

3. The assistant public prosecutor shall order the release of the suspect as soon as the interest of the investigation permits. Otherwise, he shall propose an extension of the police custody to the public prosecutor. The public prosecutor may order that the suspect be brought before him for questioning.

Translation partly borrowed from: http://www.ejtn.eu/PageFiles/6533/2014%20seminars/Omsenie/WetboekvanStrafvordering_ENG_PV.pdf. Unofficial translation; official translation not available.


This provision concerns the stage of police custody.
provisions.textEn:
1. The suspect shall be arraigned before the investigating judge in order to be heard not later than within three days and fifteen hours, to be calculated as from the time of arrest.                                                             

2. The investigating judge shall promptly set, after having received an application to that effect from the public prosecutor, the time and place at which the suspect is to be arraigned before him and he shall notify the public prosecutor, the suspect and the defence counsel thereof.

3. The suspect shall have the right to have a defence counsel present. The defence counsel shall be given the opportunity to make such comments as he sees fit during the arraignment. The public prosecutor may be present at the arraignment and make such comments as he sees fit.

4. The suspect may request the investigating judge to release him at the arraignment.

5. If the investigating judge finds that the suspect’s arrest was unlawful, he shall order his release. Otherwise, the investigating judge shall note his decision in the official record of arraignment or, if the suspect has requested his release, the investigating judge shall reject the request. The investigating judge shall certify the decision.

6. The decision shall be dated, signed and reasoned. The investigating judge shall promptly send the decision to the public prosecutor and the suspect.

Translation partly borrowed from: http://www.ejtn.eu/PageFiles/6533/2014%20seminars/Omsenie/WetboekvanStrafvordering_ENG_PV.pdf. Unofficial translation; official translation not available.


This provision concerns the stage of remand in custody.
provisions.textEn:
1. The order remanding the suspect in custody shall be in effect for a period to be set by the investigating judge, subject to a maximum of fourteen days, which shall take effect as from the time of enforcement.

2. As soon as the investigating judge or the public prosecutor is of the opinion that the grounds on which the order for remand in custody was issued no longer exist, he shall order the release of the suspect.

3. The public prosecutor may file an appeal with the District Court against the decision ordering the immediate release of the suspect given by the investigating judge under paragraph 2 within fourteen days thereafter.

This provision concerns the stages of remand detention or arrest.

Article 66a(1) of the Dutch Code of Criminal Procedure concerns the situation in which the term of vailidity of the order to remand detention or the arrest warrant has expired.
provisions.textEn:
1. The District Court may, on application of the public prosecutor, order the remand detention of the suspect who is remanded in custody. The suspect shall be heard prior to issuing such order, unless he has declared in writing that he waives his right to be heard. The District Court or the presiding judge, may, notwithstanding such declaration, order that the suspect be forcibly brought to court.
  2. Except for the case of Article 66a(1), the District Court may, ex officio or on application of the public prosecutor, after the start of the court hearing, order the arrest of the suspect. Where advisable, the District Court shall hear him beforehand; it is authorised for that purpose to order that he be summoned to appear, where necessary with an attached order that he be forcibly brought to court.
  3. The District Court may also issue a warrant of arrest, if this is necessary in order to obtain the extradition of the suspect.

Translation partly borrowed from: http://www.ejtn.eu/PageFiles/6533/2014%20seminars/Omsenie/WetboekvanStrafvordering_ENG_PV.pdf. Unofficial translation; official translation not available.


The alternative measures available under Dutch law have been enlisted in Article 27 of the Juvenile Criminal Law Decree 1994 (Besluit tenuitvoerlegging jeugdstrafrecht 1994; ﻿this is the governmental decree referred to in Article 493(6) CCP) in which it has been laid down whcih conditions can be imposed on the child upon a suspension of pre-trial detention. These conditions encompass the alternatives, referred to in the Directive.
provisions.textEn:
1. Pre-trial detention shall be determined at the shortest appropriate period of time. If the court orders the pre-trial detention of the suspect, it shall consider whether the enforcement of this order may be suspended, either immediately, or after a specific period of time. In doing so, the court may charge a foundation, as referred to in Article 1 of the Youth Care Act, or if the suspect has reached the age of sixteen years, a probation service, as referred to in Article 14d(2) of the Criminal Code, to carry out the supervision of conditions imposed on him, and, to that end, to provide support to the suspect.
  2. The order for pre-trial detention and its suspension shall include such provisions as are considered necessary for its proper enforcement.
  3. Any place suitable for such purpose may be designated as a facility for police custody or pre-trial detention. The pre-trial detention order may stipulate that the suspect stay during the night in an institution, as referred to in the Correctional Institutions for Young Offenders Framework Act, or in another place, as referred to in the first sentence, and during the day will be given the opportunity to leave the institution or that location.
  4. The duration of a remand detention order or a warrant of arrest may not exceed a period thirty days if the suspect has not been heard by the District Court.
  5. In cases where leave may be granted under the provisions laid down by or pursuant to the Correctional Institutions for Young Offenders Framework Act, the provisions of paragraphs 1 and 2 pertaining to suspension shall not apply.
  6. Suspension of the pre-trial detention shall always be subject to the general condition referred to in Article 80. The court may, after having obtained the advice of the Child Care and Protection Board, also attach special conditions to the suspension. The court shall attach special conditions to the suspension insofar as the suspect agrees to said conditions. The special conditions which may be attached to the suspension and the requirements which the agreement of the suspect must meet shall be set by Legislative Decree.
  7. The judge takes account of the age and the person of the offender, and of the circumstances under which the alleged offence has been committed.

items.comment: The stipulation in Article 493(1) of the Dutch Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP) that suspension of pre-trial detention must be considered immediately afther having been order expresses the last resort character of deprivation of liberty in the pre-trial stage of criminal proceedings against children, and, therefore the obligation to consider alternatives for deprivation of liberty. The remaining part of Article 493 CCP envisages into more detail how the procedure of suspension and the imposition of conditions shall take place.

items.heading: Article 12
items.subHeading: Specific treatment in the case of deprivation of liberty
items.comment: The official position of the Ministry of Justice and Security is that the requirements of this provision are already met by the regulations provided for in the Young Offenders Institutions (Framework) Act (Beginselenwet justitiële jeugdinrichtingen) as well as in the regulations provided for under rules adopted on the basis of this Act. The applicable provisions and rules have been set out below.

items.text: 1. Member States shall ensure that children who are detained are held separately from adults, unless it is considered to be in the child's best interests not to do so.

provisions.comment:
Own translation; no official translation available.


This provision must be read in conjunction with Article 9 of the Custodial Institutions (Framework) Act, which determines that general custodial institutions provide cells for adult suspects and adult offenders.
provisions.textEn:
Instutions are intended for:

a. Persons who have been ordered into pre-trial detention insofar at the time of the offence they allegedly committed they did not yet reach the age of 18, and persons who have been ordered into pre-trial detention insofar as the time of the offence they allegedly committed they did not yet reach the age of 23 and the public prosecutor has the intention to demand that justice will be administered in accordance with Article 77c of the Criminal Code.

[...]

provisions.comment:
Own translation; no official translation available.


This definition clarifies that police cells are intended for one single person only.
provisions.textEn: Cell: a lockable room suitable for the staying of one single person during day and night.

items.comment: The official position of the Dutch Ministry of Security and Justice is that the rule that children are detained separately from adults has already been met, since the Dutch criminal justice systems provides for specific young offenders institutions. Obviously, these young offenders institutions are exclusively intended for children. The young offenders institutions are also being used for the execution of pre-trial detention (as to which this Directive applies), except for the earliest stage of police custody. Nevertheless, the viewpoint has been taken that the requirement of separate detention is also being met in practice, simply because suspects in police custody stay in single-person-cells.

items.text: 2. Member States shall also ensure that children who are kept in police custody are held separately from adults, unless:

transp.label: No national implementation (either officially nor de facto/indirect)

items.comment: The exceptions allowed for under the Directive have not been implemented.

items.text:
(a)

it is considered to be in the child's best interests not to do so; or

transp.label: No national implementation (either officially nor de facto/indirect)

items.comment: It was chosen not to implement the exception provided for in Article 12(2)(a) of the Directive, simply because its is both stipulated and standing practice that children who are kept in pre-trial detention stay separated from adults.

items.text:
(b)

in exceptional circumstances, it is not possible in practice to do so, provided that children are held together with adults in a manner that is compatible with the child's best interests.

transp.label: No national implementation (either officially nor de facto/indirect)

items.comment: It was chosen not to implement the exception allowed under Article 12(2)(b) of the Directive, because according to the Dutch Ministry of Justice and Security, Article 37 of the International Convention on the Rights of the Child prohibits an exception on this ground.

items.text: 3. Without prejudice to paragraph 1, when a detained child reaches the age of 18, Member States shall provide for the possibility to continue to hold that person separately from other detained adults where warranted, taking into account the circumstances of the person concerned, provided that this is compatible with the best interests of children who are detained with that person.
items.comment: The Dutch Ministry of Justice and Security has pointed out that under existing legislation, it follows from the wording of Article 8 of the Young Offenders Institutions (Framework) Act (see the translation under Article 12(1) o the Directive) that children who who (allegedly) committed a crime before reaching the age of 18 and remain in pre-trial detention will stay there during the entire period of pre-trial detention.

items.text: 4. Without prejudice to paragraph 1, and taking into account paragraph 3, children may be detained with young adults, unless this is contrary to the child's best interests.

provisions.textEn:
Instutions are intended for:

a. Persons who have been ordered into pre-trial detention insofar at the time of the offence they allegedly committed they did not yet reach the age of 18, and persons who have been ordered into pre-trial detention insofar as the time of the offence they allegedly committed they did not yet reach the age of 23 and the public prosecutor has the intention to demand that justice will be administered in accordance with Article 77c of the Criminal Code.

items.comment: Article 8 of the Young Offenders Institutions (Framework) Act also applies to suspects below 23 years old whose pre-trial detention has been order, but as to whom the public prosecutor intends to request in court that their cases will be tried in accordance with the provisions applicable to children. Consequently, it may occur that children and young adults remain in the same youth offenders institution.

items.text: 5. When children are detained, Member States shall take appropriate measures to:
items.comment: The official position of the Dutch Ministry of Justice and Security is that the rights provided for in the various subsections of Article 12(5) of the Directive already follow from existing legislation. The applicable provisions have been set out below.

items.text:
(a)

ensure and preserve their health and their physical and mental development;

provisions.comment:
Own translation; no official translation available.


This provision determines in general terms the purpose to use any deprivation of liberty - including in the pre-trial stage of criminal proceedings - for the purpose of education and rehabilitation.
provisions.textEn: Without prejudice to the nature of a custodial sentence or custodial measure, its execution shall be used for the education of the juvenile and shall as much as possible be made to be conducive to his return to society. If a custodial measure entails treatment, its execution shall be accommodated accordingly. In granting freedoms to juveniles, due consideration shall be given to the security of society and the interests of victims and their relatives.

provisions.comment: Translation partly borrowed from the almost equally worded provision in the Penitentiairy Principles Act, Article 41 (Penitentiaire Beginselenwet): http://www.legislationline.org/documents/action/popup/id/4692. Unofficial translation; official translation not available.
provisions.textEn:
1. The juveline shall have a right to freely profess and practice his religion or ideology individually or in association with others.

2. The governor shall provide that sufficient spiritual care, as much as possible in accordance with the juvenile's religion or ideology, is available in the institution.

3. The governor shall give the juvenile the opportunity at the times and places laid down in the prison rules to:

a. have personal contact with the spiritual counsellor of the religion or ideology of his choice connected with the institution;

b. have contact with persons other than the spiritual counsellors referred to under a pursuant to Article 43;

c. attend the religious or ideological meetings of his choice held in the institution. Article 24 shall apply mutatis mutandis.

4. Further rules shall be established by order in council concerning the availability of spiritual care. These rules shall refer to the provision of spiritual care by or on behalf of the different religious or ideological movements, to the organisation and the cost of spiritual care and to the appointment of spiritual counsellors in an institution.

provisions.comment: Translation partly borrowed from the almost equally worded provision in the Penitentiairy Principles Act, Article 42 (Penitentiaire Beginselenwet): http://www.legislationline.org/documents/action/popup/id/4692. Unofficial translation; official translation not available.
provisions.textEn:
1. The juvenile shall have a right to receive the care of a physician connected with the institution or his substitute.

2. The juvenile shall have a right to consult, at his own expense, a physician of his choice. The governor shall establish the place and time of the consultation, in consultation with the chosen physician.

3. The governor shall provide that the physician connected with the institution or his substitute:

a. is regularly available for holding surgery hours;

b. is available at other times if this is necessary in the interest of the juvenile's health;

c. examines the juveniles that are eligible for this for their fitness to participate in work, sport or other activities.

4.The governor shall provide that:

a. the juvenile is provided with the drugs and diets prescribed by the physician connected with the institution or his substitute;

items.comment: The official position of the Dutch Ministry of Justice and Security is that existing legislation already meets the requirement under Article 12(6) of the Directive. Article 490(3) of the Dutch Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP) declares that in criminal proceedings against children, Article 45 CCP applies with respect to the parents and the guardian of the child. Article 45 CCP deals with free access of laywers to their clients who have been deprived of their liberty. Pursuant to Article 490(3) CCP, parents and guardians have free access too. However, because Article 490(3) CCP does not apply to suspects kept in youth offender institutions, the question arises whether and to what extent Article 490(3) in conjunction with Article 45 CCP actually fully comply with the Directive. To our assessment, Article 490(3) CCP only partially implements the Directive.

items.heading: Article 13
items.subHeading: Timely and diligent treatment of cases
items.comment: The Dutch Ministry of Justice and Security has taken te position that implementation is not required. See comments with respect to the respective paragrahps which, in relation to paragraph 2, leads to our conclusion that this paragraph must actually be considered indirectly/de facto implemented. However, we have chosen not to include all provisions that constitute such an indirect/de facto implementation of Article 13(2) of the Directive, because of the likelihood that we will be too extensive, still not exhaustive.

items.text: 1. Member States shall take all appropriate measures to ensure that criminal proceedings involving children are treated as a matter of urgency and with due diligence.
items.comment: The Dutch Ministry of Justice and Security has taken te position that implementation is not required. It states that Article 13(1) of the Directive concerns the speed and diligence with which criminal proceedings against children must proceed, and that both of these norms - despite their being not codified in Dutch law - anyhow provide essential starting points of Dutch criminal procedure. Moreover, it is standing case law of the Supreme Court of the Netherlands that criminal proceedings against children must in principle be concluded within 16 months (against 24 months for adults, see https://uitspraken.rechtspraak.nl/inziendocument?id=ECLI:NL:HR:2015:2465, in Dutch only). The Dutch Public Prosecution Service has committed to meet this term in 80% of the juvenile criminal cases (Article 6, Richtlijn en kader voor strafvordering jeugd en adolescenten, inclusief strafmaten Halt, Staatscourant 2018, 29497, https://wetten.overheid.nl/BWBR0040956/2018-06-01, in Dutch only). It has therefore been held that with the available manpower in the Dutch criminal justice system, Article 13(1) of the Directive is being met as much as possible.

items.text: 2. Member States shall take appropriate measures to ensure that children are always treated in a manner which protects their dignity and which is appropriate to their age, maturity and level of understanding, and which takes into account any special needs, including any communication difficulties, that they may have.
items.comment: As stated by the Dutch Ministry of Justice, the very starting point of juvenile criminal proceedings is to ensure due account of their age, personality and other special needs. This follows from various provisions throughout the Dutch Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP), especially those that have been laid down in Title II of Book 4 that contains a number of provisions that specifically apply to criminal proceedings against minor suspects (Article 488 et seq.), see for instance Articles 493(7), 494a(2) and 494b CCP. It was therefore held that no explicit implementation was necessary.

items.text: 1. Member States shall ensure that children have the right to be present at their trial and shall take all necessary measures to enable them to participate effectively in the trial, including by giving them the opportunity to be heard and to express their views.

Note that Dutch law compels suspects to be present during court hearings, whereas the Directive envisages a right thereto.
provisions.textEn:
1. The suspect shall be obliged to appear in person. He shall be notified by summons that if he does not comply with this obligation, the court may order that he be brought forcibly.

2. If the person suspected of having committed a serious offence fails to appear at the court session, the court shall, unless nullity and voidness of the summons, a bar to the prosecution or lack of jurisdiction of the court is immediately apparent, adjourn the hearing to a specific date and shall also order that the suspect be brought forcibly to court. However, the court may decline to issue an order to forcibly bring the suspect to court if the suspect has no known place of residence or abode or on the grounds of special reasons.

3. The suspect who fails to comply with the order to appear before the court shall be tried in absentia, unless the court orders that he be brought forcibly to court at a later date. The hearing shall then be continued.

4. Paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 shall not apply if at the time of the court session the suspect has since reached the age of eighteen years.

provisions.textEn:
Upon arrest, the requested person shall be promptly informed in writing of:

a) the right to receive a copy of the European arrest warrant, as referred to in Article 23(3);

b) the right of access to a lawyer, as referred to in Article 43a, and the possibility to request the appointment of a lawyer in the issuing Member State, as referred to in Article 21a;

c) the right to interpretation, as referred to in Article 30, and the right to translation, as provided for under Article 23(3), fourth and fifth sentences;

d) the right to be heard, as referred to in Article 24;

e) the rights referred to in Article 27c(3) under g and h of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

The requested person who does not have a sufficient command of Dutch shall be informed of his rights in a language he understands. Articles 27e, 488ab, and 488b Code of Criminal Procedure shall apply accordingly.

This provision is considered to meet the requirement to provide requested persons in EAW proceedings with the right of legal assistance, as referred to in Article 6 of the Directive.
provisions.textEn:
1. In the proceedings for surrender of a person by the Netherlands, the requested person has the right to be assisted by a lawyer. Articles 28, 28a, 28c(2), 29a(1), 37, 38, 43 to 45 and 124 of the Code of Criminal Procedure shall apply mutatis mutandis.
  2. If a requested person is arrested pursuant to this statute, the assistant public prosecutor shall notify the governing body of the Legal Aid Board thereof, in order that the governing body appoints a lawyer. Articles 28b(1), second sentence, and 39 of the Code of Criminal Procedure shall apply mutatis mutandis.
  3. If the lawyer is not available within two hours of the notification as per the second paragraph being given, the public prosecutor or, with the public prosecutor's permission, the assistant public prosecutor, may begin questioning the requested person in connection with the decision on whether to take them into police custody within the meaning of Article 17(4) and 21(5).
  4. The requested person in respect of whom a lawyer is available pursuant to the second paragraph, shall be given the opportunity to consult with their lawyer prior to questioning in connection with the decision to be taken within the meaning of the third paragraph for a maximum of half an hour.
  5. If a person who does not have a lawyer pursuant to this statute is deprived of their liberty - other than pursuant to a European arrest warrant or a Dutch warrant of arrest or provisional arrest, or an order to be taken into police custody or for such custody to be extended - the governing body of the Legal Aid Board shall, upon notification of the deprivation of liberty by the Public Prosecution Service, appoint a lawyer.

This provision further establishes the application of Article 11 of the Directive in EAW proceedings which stipulates to have recourse to measures alternative to detention. After all, an equal treatment of reqeusted persons and 'normal' suspects incudes equal recourse to suspending pre-trial detention and to impose conditions (supervision measures) on the person involved.


Moreover, this provision also established the application of the right to a specific treatment in EAW proceedings (Article 12 of the Directive).  The envisaged equal treatment of requested persons and suspects in the sense of the Dutch Code of Criminal Procedure also means that children in detention receive a specific treatment. See further the comments made with respect to the transposition of Article 12 of the Directive.

This provision means to apply Article 15 of the Directive (the right to be accompanied by parents, etc. during proceedings) in EAW proceedings. It must be read in conjunction with Articles 21(10), 24(4) and 25(5) of the Surrender of Persons Act, which alltogether establish the transposition of this right in various stages of the surrender proceedings.


Article 490(1) first ful sentence and (3) of the Dutch Code of Criminal Procedure read as follows:


1.Notwithstanding Article 59(5) the Child Care and Protection Board shall be promptly notified of the suspect being taken in police custody.

[...]

3.If the suspect has been deprived of his liberty by law and has not been placed in a correctional institution for young offenders, Article 45 shall apply mutatis mutandis in regard of his parents or his guardian.


Note that Article 490(3) of the Dutch Code of Criminal Procedure (CCP) declares that in criminal proceedings against children, Article 45 CCP applies with respect to the parents and the guardian of the child. Article 45 CCP deals with free access of laywers to their clients who have been deprived of their liberty. Pursuant to Article 490(3) CCP, parents and guardians have free access too. Under Article 62 of the Surrender of Persons Act, this is now also the case in surrender proceedings. As already explained with respect to Article 15 itself, Article 62 of the Surrender of Persons Act must be considered a partial implementation, for 490(3) CCP does not apply to suspects kept in youth offender institutions. , the question arises whether and to what extent Article 490(3) in conjunction with Article 45 CCP actually fully comply with the Directive. To our assessment, Article 490(3) CCP only partially implements the Directive.
provisions.textEn: Article 490, paragraph 1, first full sentence, and paragraph 3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure shall apply mutatis mutandis
